title: Where AI Fits in Brand and Product Design

slide.title: Where Does AI Fit?
slide.body: A six-stage design process line (Research to Delivery); three stages glow teal, one carries a small 'No AI' tag. Small tag: AI for Brand and Product Design · Lesson 1.

production_notes: No facts to verify: the lesson teaches general principles with a hypothetical example (content.md Review Flags: None).
Mateo Rojas and the bakery chain in Santiago are fictional; stock footage must not show a real bakery name, shop sign or logo.
Figma AI features are mentioned only in passing; no product claims are made in this lesson.

Hook.voiceover: An AI tool can give you forty logo ideas in a minute. It can also give you forty ideas that look like marks you have seen before, in colours that fail a contrast check. The skill is knowing where AI helps, and where it hurts.
Hook.on_screen_text: Where does AI help, and hurt?

Explain.voiceover: Hi, and welcome to AI for Brand and Product Design. In this first lesson, we draw a map. Where does AI fit in your design process, and where should it stay out?

slide.title: Where AI Fits in Brand and Product Design
slide.body: AI for Brand and Product Design · Lesson 1 of 14

Explain.voiceover: You already know the design process. Most brand and product projects move through similar stages. Research, definition, ideation, design and systems, prototyping and testing, and finally delivery. AI can take part in every stage, but it does not add the same value at each one.

slide.title: The design process
slide.body: Six boxes in a line, revealed one by one: Research → Definition (insights, personas, brief) → Ideation (names, moodboards, concepts) → Design and systems → Prototyping and testing → Delivery (files, guidelines, handover)

Explain.voiceover: AI adds the most value where the work needs volume, speed or variation. Volume means summarising thirty interview transcripts, or drafting fifty name options. Speed means turning a rough idea into a first layout or a moodboard in minutes instead of hours. Variation means showing you directions you would not have tried.

slide.title: Where AI adds value
slide.body: Volume: 30 transcripts summarised, 50 name options · Speed: rough idea to first layout in minutes · Variation: directions you would not have tried

Explain.voiceover: AI adds the most risk where the work needs originality, accuracy or rights. Image generators learn from huge sets of existing images, so their output can drift towards clichés, or look close to existing marks. Language models can invent quotes, or suggest a colour pair that looks accessible but is not. And AI cannot tell you whether a name is free to use.

slide.title: Where AI adds risk
slide.body: Originality: drift to clichés, close to existing marks · Accuracy: invented quotes, 'accessible-looking' colours that fail · Rights: AI cannot clear a name

Explain.voiceover: There is also judgement. Choosing which insight matters and which direction fits the client is your job. AI can argue for options, but it does not carry responsibility for the result. You do.
Explain.on_screen_text: AI suggests. You carry the responsibility.

Explain.voiceover: Here is a helpful way to picture it. Think of AI as a fast junior assistant on your team. The assistant works quickly, never gets tired and produces many options. But it has no memory of your client meetings, sometimes invents details with confidence, and does not know the law.
Explain.stock_query: senior designer reviewing junior colleague work

Explain.voiceover: You would never send a junior's first draft to a client without a senior review. So treat every AI output in the same way.

slide.title: The senior review
slide.body: Every AI output gets a senior review before a client sees it.

Explain.voiceover: Now, mark each stage with one of three labels. The first is AI drafts, I decide. AI produces options, and you select and refine. The second is AI checks, I own. You do the work, and AI reviews it for gaps. The third is no AI, for confidential data, final legal decisions and relationships with people.

slide.title: Three labels for every stage
slide.body: Three columns: 'AI drafts, I decide' (ideation, microcopy) · 'AI checks, I own' (briefs, critique) · 'No AI' (confidential data, legal decisions, relationships)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see this in practice. Mateo Rojas is a freelance product designer in Santiago, Chile. His client, a small chain of bakeries, wants a new brand and a simple ordering app. So Mateo maps his usual process, and marks each stage.
Demonstrate.stock_query: freelance product designer working laptop studio

Demonstrate.voiceover: He does the customer interviews himself, with no AI, because relationships and consent matter. For research synthesis, AI drafts and he decides. Claude groups his anonymised notes into themes, and he checks every quote. For the brief, AI checks and he owns. Claude asks critical questions about his draft.

slide.title: Mateo's AI plan, part 1
slide.body: Table with three rows: Customer interviews → No AI (relationships, consent) · Research synthesis → AI drafts, I decide (checks every quote) · Brief → AI checks, I own (critical questions)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Names and moodboards get AI drafts. The final logo gets no AI. He redraws the chosen concept by hand in Figma. For the UI screens, Figma's AI features give a first layout, and he rebuilds it with his own components. And trademark checks get no AI at all. They need official searches, and possibly a lawyer.

slide.title: Mateo's AI plan, part 2
slide.body: Table continues: Names and moodboards → AI drafts, I decide · Logo final art → No AI (redrawn in Figma) · UI screens → AI drafts, I decide (rebuilt with his components) · Trademark checks → No AI (official searches, lawyer)

Demonstrate.voiceover: Mateo notices something. His plan uses AI in more than half of the stages. But the decisions stay with him at every stage. He writes the plan into his project notes, so he can explain his process to the client later.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: AI in most stages. Decisions in all.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to treat AI as a yes or no choice for the whole project. Decide stage by stage instead. And do not measure AI only by speed. A fast draft that needs three rounds of fixing is not faster.

slide.title: Not all or nothing
slide.body: Left (red cross): 'AI for the whole project' or 'no AI at all'. Right (green tick): decide the AI role stage by stage, and who reviews it. Footer: a fast draft that needs three rounds of fixes is not faster.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, AI adds value where design work needs volume, speed or variation. Second, AI adds risk where the work needs originality, accuracy or rights, so those outputs always need human checks. Third, plan AI use stage by stage, with clear roles. AI drafts, I decide. AI checks, I own. Or no AI.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Value: volume, speed, variation. 2. Risk: originality, accuracy, rights, so always check. 3. Plan stage by stage: AI drafts, I decide · AI checks, I own · No AI

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will map your own design process. Mark three steps where AI could help, and one step where you would not use it, with your reasons. It takes about twenty minutes. In the next lesson, we look at research synthesis with Claude. See you there.
